newsitem.title: UK: British scientists find more signs of life on Mars.
newsitem.headline: British scientists find more signs of life on Mars.

text.p: British astronomers said on Thursday they had found new evidence to back reports from U.S. space scientists that traces of life had been found in a meteorite from Mars.

They said samples from two separate Martian meteorites showed definite traces that could have been left by living organisms, and one was recent enough to indicate that there still could be life surviving somewhere on Mars.
"We think that this is backing for the supposition that there is life on Mars," Colin Pillinger, an astronomer at Britain's Open University, told a news conference.
Pillinger said his team had taken a closer look at a sample from the meteorite -- known as ALH84001 -- that the U.S. space agency NASA said contained traces of life.
That sample, he said, contained a carbon isotope -- a variant of carbon -- that is often produced by microscopic life forms on Earth.
NASA startled the world last August when it said chemicals in its sample of ALH84001 could have been left by tiny bacteria.
Studies published since then questioned that finding, some saying the little holes in the ancient Mars rock seemed to have been formed at temperatures too extreme for life to survive.
But Pillinger said his group had found carbon 12 in the sample.
"On Earth the only thing you find that is enriched with carbon 12 is methane produced by microbial action," he said. Examples would be tiny bacteria that live in cows' stomachs and rice paddy fields.
He told the news conference there had been a lot of criticism of the NASA announcement. "We felt there was a danger of interest slipping away."
So they called a conference of experts on space exploration, extraterrestrial life, astronomy, biology and other subjects.
Partly in preparation for Thursday's conference, his group re-examined old meteorites they had after NASA's announcement last summer. They were stunned by what they found.
"We have identified a second meteorite which appears to contain matter that we define as organic," Pillinger said. "We have not yet homed in on the nature of the organic matter involved."
He urged other scientists to get samples from NASA and study just what the meteorites do contain. NASA is studying requests for samples of its Martian meteorites.
NASA's meteorite is believed to have been knocked off Mars by an asteroid and thrown into orbit 16 million years ago.
The second meteorite, known as EETA79001, is much younger and could have been knocked away only 600,000 years ago.
"This throws it into a time when life would have been teeming on Earth," Pillinger said.
"Geologically speaking this is sufficiently recent for there to be a good chance that life might still exist in protected areas on our planetary neighbour."
Pillinger acknowledged that his group's findings had not undergone the normal scientific processes of peer review and publication that lend weight to any such study.
"We felt it was right of us to bring these facts to you as soon as we possibly could," he said.
